one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a jurisprudential meditation: most judges apply Austin's Analytical School formula -- law times fact equals decision (LxF=D) -- taught consciously or unconsciously in most law schools, where students master codes, statutes, and precedents and apply them to hypothetical facts under verba legis discipline, with departures denounced as 'judicial legislation' and bad results shrugged off as 'dura lex sed lex.' This formula, he shows, reduces decision-making to an Aristotelian syllogism: 'Anyone who kills shall be jailed; Pedro killed Juan; ergo, Pedro goes to jail.' Like math, the formula is consistent in the abstract -- but math itself fails in reality: one drop of water plus another is not two drops but one bigger drop; one piece of wood divided by four is not one-fourth but four smaller pieces. Two problems plague Austin's formula. First, no science assures discovery of 'the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth' -- witnesses lie, forget, confuse, or fail to observe; documents are incomplete, vague, or fake; scientific and historical evidence is faultily extracted or badly preserved. Second, laws themselves are incomplete, unclear, confusing, contradictory, or obsolete. Textualists default at this point and say what's outside the text is outside legal contemplation -- but justice must be served. The Civil Code itself forecloses this hand-washing: 'No judge or court shall decline to render judgment by reason of the silence, obscurity or insufficiency of the laws,' and 'in case of doubt in the interpretation or application of laws, it is presumed that the lawmaking body intended right and justice to prevail.' When verba legis fails, great jurists rise -- they search 'beyond the text' in six sources: (1) overarching constitutional principles, (2) grand intentions of the framers, (3) great judicial axioms, (4) landmark precedents, (5) international conventions, (6) legal presumptions. He applies this toolkit to Grace Poe's case, which presents 'a rare moment for judicial greatness': the texts of governing laws neither include nor exclude foundlings; her residency facts are torn between her mistaken 2013 COC computation and the truth that she had actually transferred her domicile to the Philippines in 2005. He enumerates six pillars favoring her: (1) as a foundling, she deserves the social-justice principle of giving 'more law to those who have less in life'; (2) the 1935 Constitution framers explicitly stated it was never their intention 'to exclude foundlings from natural-born citizenship'; (3) the grand axiom Salus populi est suprema lex may be invoked extra-constitutionally to render social justice, famously wrote 'the eminent Justice Jose P. Laurel'; (4) Frivaldo vs Comelec teaches that doubt in interpretation favors enabling the electorate's free choice, Bengzon vs HRET affirms that repatriated natural-born Filipinos reacquire their original citizenship, and Marcos vs Comelec instructs that truth (not mistaken COC statements) prevails; (5) the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the covenants on civil and political rights, on the reduction of statelessness, and on the rights of the child all favor foundlings; (6) presumptions of good faith, nondiscrimination, and regularity in performance of duties undoubtedly benefit her. Judging from the 'gutsy Comment' filed by SG Florin Hilbay, Panganiban believes he too has seen the moment for judicial greatness -- and given Hilbay's sterling track record as bar topnotcher and law professor and Panganiban's personal knowledge of his writing ability and excellent reports as a court attorney 15 years ago, if Hilbay were a sitting jurist he could 'rise to the moment and craft a grand historic decision.'
